items.title: FinCEN & OFAC propose GENIUS Act AML/sanctions rules for stablecoin issuers
items.summary: On 8 Apr 2026 FinCEN and OFAC issued a joint NPRM implementing the GENIUS Act: permitted payment stablecoin issuers (PPSIs) would be treated as BSA 'financial institutions', must run AML/CFT programmes and — for the first time — maintain an explicit sanctions-compliance programme. Final rules take effect 12 months after issuance.
items.soWhat: Stablecoin issuers become regulated FIs with their own sanctions duties — counterparty risk on compliant issuers falls, but expect them to wield freeze/seize powers; align issuer-freeze playbooks now.

items.title: Pig-butchering 2026: agentic AI grooming, approval-phishing drains, and Southeast Asia scam-centre strikes
items.summary: Pig-butchering has industrialised in 2026. Criminal syndicates now deploy agentic AI to run thousands of simultaneous grooming relationships, pushing average scam payouts up 253% year-on-year (from $782 to $2,764 per transaction). The attack endgame has shifted to 'approval phishing' — victims are manipulated into signing wallet-spending permissions that attackers drain weeks later, bypassing conventional 'send crypto' red flags. In April 2026, DOJ, OFAC, and State launched a coordinated multi-pronged strike against Southeast Asian scam centres; Operation Atlantic (March 2026) targeted approval-phishing victims alongside UK NCA and Canadian authorities.
items.soWhat: AI-enabled scale means scam-proceeds volumes will keep rising even as individual victim counts plateau — expect higher-value SARs from investment-fraud flows. Approval-phishing bypasses typical transaction monitoring; update typologies to flag repeated ERC-20 token-approval contract interactions from retail wallets. Downstream laundering flows through Chinese-language money laundering networks (see feed-chinese-mln-laas-typology), so pig-butchering proceeds and CLMN cluster screening should be treated as coupled intelligence.

items.title: Treasury GENIUS Act tech report: AI-powered crypto oversight and a proposed 'digital-asset hold law'
items.summary: On 6 March 2026, Treasury published its congressionally-mandated report on innovative technologies to counter illicit finance in digital assets under the GENIUS Act. The report endorses AI, digital identity, blockchain analytics, and APIs as priority compliance tools, and proposes a legislative 'digital-asset hold law' safe harbour — allowing financial institutions to temporarily freeze suspicious crypto transactions without liability while investigations proceed. Treasury also signalled a nuanced shift on mixers, acknowledging legitimate privacy use cases rather than treating all mixer-touched funds as presumptively illicit.
items.soWhat: The proposed hold-law safe harbour removes a key legal barrier for proactive crypto intervention, directly reinforcing the on-ledger enforcement thesis already in Treasury's NPRM (see feed-treasury-programmable-enforcement). For bank compliance teams, the report is also a forward indicator for supervisory expectations: AI-assisted transaction monitoring and blockchain analytics are being positioned as required capabilities, not differentiators. The mixer nuance matters too — blanket mixer-flag policies may need recalibration against a mixed-use risk-based standard.

items.title: Ransomware laundering pivots from mixers to cross-chain bridges: 66% bridge surge, 37% mixer decline
items.summary: TRM Labs' 2026 Crypto Crime Report documents a sharp behavioural shift in ransomware post-payment laundering across 2024-25: bridge-related activity grew 66% while mixer use fell 37%, as threat actors adapted to OFAC sanctions against Tornado Cash and heightened mixer monitoring. Ransomware itself is growing — 93 new variants emerged (a 94% jump) and $820M in payments were recorded in 2025. Cross-chain bridges offer routing flexibility and liquidity-venue diversity that is structurally harder to trace via wallet-level blockchain analytics.
items.soWhat: Detection rules anchored to mixer-flag typologies are increasingly stale for ransomware proceeds. Update transaction monitoring to flag multi-hop cross-chain bridge sequences — particularly patterns that hop tokens across chains before converging on an exchange deposit address. The 94% jump in active ransomware strains also means the incoming volume of laundering flows to the financial system is growing; expect higher SAR volumes from this vector.

items.title: DPRK's Drift and KelpDAO exploits claim 76% of all 2026 crypto hack losses — $577M via protocol-level compromise
items.summary: Two North Korean operations in April 2026 — Drift ($285M, April 1) and KelpDAO ($290M, April 18) — captured 76% of all crypto hack losses year-to-date and pushed DPRK cumulative theft past $6 billion since 2017. The Drift attack involved months of in-person social engineering to compromise Solana multisig signers, executing a 12-minute drain; KelpDAO was exploited via a single-verifier LayerZero bridge flaw. Laundering diverged: Drift proceeds remain dormant; KelpDAO funds (after $75M were frozen on Arbitrum) were routed through THORChain and converted to Bitcoin via Chinese intermediaries using the TraderTraitor playbook.
items.soWhat: DPRK has shifted decisively to DeFi protocol-level compromise — achieving $500M+ single incidents via governance attacks and bridge exploits rather than exchange hacks alone. Banks should screen for THORChain-to-Bitcoin conversion patterns tied to the April 2026 addresses, assess any counterparty exposure to Drift or KelpDAO recovery flows, and treat dormant DPRK holdings as a deferred laundering risk that will hit the financial system on DPRK's timetable.

items.title: CertiK: A7A5 hits $110B cumulative, 43% of non-USD stablecoin market — no kill-switch makes sanctions structurally ineffective
items.summary: CertiK's Skynet 2026 Stablecoin Threat Intelligence Report found A7A5 processed over $110 billion in cumulative on-chain transactions between February 2025 and May 2026, capturing 43% of the global non-USD stablecoin market. Active wallets grew from 13,000 to 29,000 in the period. Critically, A7A5 was designed without a centralised kill-switch — smart contracts are controlled by Russian and Kyrgyz developers; reserves sit in Central Asian banking networks beyond Western reach. Despite the UK's May 2026 OFSI designation and the EU 20th package prohibition, daily volume fell only from a $1.5B peak to approximately $500M.
items.soWhat: A7A5's 43% non-USD stablecoin market share reframes it from a niche evasion tool to a systemically significant parallel settlement rail. The absence of a kill-switch makes issuer-level sanctions structurally ineffective at stopping flows — the only reliable controls are blocking the fiat on/off ramps (Grinex, TengriCoin, Central Asian banking channels). Banks should treat any A7A5-denominated settlement or Grinex counterparty exposure as equivalent to direct Russia sanctions risk and prioritise on-chain screening of known A7A5 broker clusters.

items.title: FinCEN Section 311 severs Swiss MBaer Merchant Bank from US system — FINMA orders liquidation
items.summary: On 26 February 2026, FinCEN proposed the most severe Section 311 measure against MBaer Merchant Bank AG, a Swiss private bank, prohibiting US financial institutions from opening or maintaining correspondent accounts for it and requiring enhanced due diligence against indirect access. FinCEN alleged MBaer funnelled over $100M through the US financial system on behalf of Iranian and Russian illicit actors — including $50M+ in Iranian oil smuggling — as well as Venezuelan corruption and terrorist financing. For UK/EU banks, the lesson is that a small private bank with concentrated high-risk client exposure and lax controls can be severed from the dollar system with no grandfathering period. Review any correspondent banking or sub-custodian relationships with Swiss private banks that have material CIS/Russia/Iran-nexus client books — the MBaer precedent signals FinCEN is prepared to use its most severe tool against non-US banks.

items.title: CLARITY Act reaches US Senate floor calendar — 8 weeks to pass or die before summer recess
items.summary: The Digital Asset Market Clarity Act cleared the Senate Banking Committee 15–9 on 14 May 2026 and was formally placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar on 1 June 2026. The bill would resolve the SEC/CFTC jurisdiction standoff by routing every digital asset into one of three categories: digital commodities (CFTC exclusive jurisdiction), investment-contract assets (SEC), and permitted payment stablecoins (joint oversight). It faces a narrow runway — approximately eight weeks of Senate floor time before the summer recess — and needs 60 votes, requiring at least seven Democrats. The principal sticking point is an ethics provision mandating that the President and senior officials divest personal crypto holdings; without it, Democrats call the bill a dealbreaker. Galaxy Digital has reportedly bet $10M on 2026 passage.
items.soWhat: Passage would end five years of enforcement-by-litigation uncertainty on the securities/commodity classification question — materially reducing regulatory risk for US-facing crypto counterparties and reshaping what 'compliant' means for exchange and token products. Failure (or a thin partisan passage) leaves the SEC/CFTC ambiguity intact and signals continued litigation-as-regulation. Banks with US digital-asset exposure should treat the ethics-provision resolution as the leading indicator: a bipartisan deal implies durable certainty; a party-line result implies fragility.

items.title: Kroll: US AML fines declining as illicit crypto flows hit record $158B — deregulation widens enforcement gap
items.summary: Kroll's March 2026 report 'The Money Laundering Surge: Crypto, Enforcement Gaps and What Comes Next' documents a structural mismatch: crypto-linked illicit flows reached an estimated record $158 billion in 2025 — more than twice 2024's total — while global AML fines and penalties declined, especially in the US. Kroll attributes the enforcement gap to deregulatory trends, FinCEN staff reductions, and a fragmented state-level money transmitter licence framework that leaves crypto exchanges — handling trillions annually — subject to rarer and less rigorous federal examination than banks. AI-powered automation is identified as a key driver of the surge in laundering sophistication.
items.soWhat: A record illicit-flow number alongside declining US enforcement creates a de facto permissiveness signal that sophisticated laundering networks will exploit. For UK/EU institutions, the US enforcement gap means US-origin counterparties and correspondent flows warrant heightened scrutiny, not reduced, even as domestic US regulatory noise quietens under the Trump administration. The Kroll finding also validates the European approach of tightening (AMLA, MiCA) as a competitive differentiator — expect divergent standards between the US and EU crypto compliance regimes to widen further in 2026–27.
